sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Sarutahiko** ​(*sarutahiko*) — ‌Crossroads, Guidance ‌· ​Monkey-field prince ​— belongs ​to ​the Japanese ​tradition, where ‌it ​is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Crossroads, Guidance". ‌The ​name means ‌"Monkey-field prince"[^1].

​**Sarutahiko** ​is the ​kami who ​stands ​at the ‌boundary between ​heaven ‌and earth. ​When Ninigi ‌descended ​from Takamagahara, ‌Sarutahiko ​blocked the ‌way until ​Ame-no-Uzume ​persuaded him ‌to become ‌the ‌guide. With ​his long ​nose, ‌glaring eyes, ​and red ​face, ‌he became ​the model ​for ‌the *taikomochi* ​and ‌*tenjin* figures ​of Japanese ​folk ​performance and ​the patron ‌of ‌those who ​stand at ‌thresholds.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the name ‌as ‌**Sarutahiko** and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/sarutahiko/). ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ‌a description ​computed from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*sarutahiko* survives ‌as ​a modern ‌convenience imposed ​by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Japanese characters ​as ​**猿田彦**. Etymologically ​it ​means ‌"Monkey-field prince"[^1].

​The ​ASCII form ‌*sarutahiko* ​survives ‌only because ​the ‌early domain-name ​system ​could ​not carry ​diacritics; ​it is ‌a ​technological ‌compromise, not ​an ‌ancient spelling. ​The ‌Unicode ​restoration **Sarutahiko** ‌recovers ​the full ​diacritic ‌detail ‌of the ‌scholarly ​transliteration directly ​in ‌the ​address bar. ​The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— ‌a description ​computed ‌from ​the displayed ​form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation ‌runs:

- **s** ​→ ‌**S** — ​Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**a** → ‌**a** ‌— Same
- ‌**r** ​→ ‌**r** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/sa.ɾɯ.ta.hi.ko/** — ​Modern Standard ​Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Sa-** ‌— Voiceless ​alveolar fricative ​[s] plus ‌open central ​[a]
- ‌**-ru-** — ​Alveolar tap ‌[ɾ] plus ​close back ​unrounded [ɯ]
- ​**-ta-** — ​Voiceless alveolar ​stop [t] ‌plus open ​central [a]; ‌from 田 ​'field'
- ‌**-hiko** — ​Voiceless glottal ‌[h], close ​front [i], ‌voiceless velar ​[k], open-mid ​[o]; from ‌彦 'prince/lad'

‌For the ‌modern speaker, ​the closest ​approximation is: ‌'SAH-roo-tah-hee-koh' ​— the ​'r' is ‌a light ​tap, and ​all vowels ‌are short.

​Kindred and ‌historical forms ​of the ​name:

- **Japanese** ​— 猿田彦 ​(Sarutahiko) ‌— saru ‌'monkey' + ​ta 'field' ‌+ hiko ​'prince'; the ​saruta element ‌is etymologically ‌obscure (Ashkenazi, ‌Handbook of ‌Japanese Mythology).
- ​**Wife** — ‌Ame-no-Uzume-no-mikoto, the ​dancing ​goddess; the ​Kojiki makes ‌her the ​ancestress of ​the Sarume.
- ​**Descendants** — ‌The Sarume ​(猿女, 'monkey-women') ​clan of ​female ritual ‌dancers, from ​whom ‌the kagura ​tradition descends ‌(Kojiki).

Sarutahiko ​keeps its ‌restoration plain: ‌plain Hepburn. ​He is ​the kami ​who guided ​Ninigi's descent ‌and who ‌stands at ​boundaries.

sections.body:
**Sarutahiko** ​is ‌the ‌kami ​who stands ​at ​the ​boundary ​between ‌heaven ​and ​earth. When ‌Ninigi ​descended ‌from ​Takamagahara, ‌Sarutahiko ​blocked ​the way ​until ​Ame-no-Uzume ​persuaded ‌him ​to ‌become ​the ‌guide. With ​his ‌long ​nose, ‌glaring ​eyes, ​and ‌red face, ‌he ‌became ​the ​model ‌for ​the ​*taikomochi* and ‌*tenjin* ​figures ​of ‌Japanese ​folk ‌performance ​and ​the patron ​of ​those ‌who ‌stand ​at ‌thresholds.[^1]

### ​Guide of ​Ninigi

‌He ‌led ‌Ninigi's ‌descent ​from ‌heaven to ​earth.

### ​Crossroads ​Guardian

‌He ​protects ​boundaries, ​paths, ‌and transitions.

### ​Husband ​of ​Uzume

‌Ame-no-Uzume ​married ‌him ​after negotiating ‌the ​heavenly ‌descent.

### ‌Folk ​Performer

​His ​appearance influenced ​comedic ‌and ‌ceremonial ​performers.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Sarutahiko's mythology is compact but ​complete in its own way: the earth-born kami ‌who blocks the heavenly descent and becomes its ‌guide; the husband of the dancing goddess; a ​drowned god whose spirit is still named at ​Ise. Around these Kojiki and Nihon Shoki episodes, ​folk religion built a vast afterlife of crossroads, ​masks, and martial arts.[^1]

### The Blockade at the ​Floating Bridge (Kojiki / Nihon Shoki)

When Ninigi ‌no Mikoto, grandson of Amaterasu, prepared to descend ​from Takamagahara to rule the Central Land of ​Reed-Plains, an awesome figure stood at the eight-fold ‌crossroads at the earthward end of the Floating ​Bridge of Heaven. The *Kojiki* describes Sarutahiko with a ‌long nose, a red and shining face, eyes ​like eight-span mirrors, and a beard that hung ‌down; the *Nihon Shoki* variant measures him more ​exactly — a nose of seven hand-spans, a ​height over seven feet, eyes red like mirrors ​— and says the heavenly envoys sent to ​negotiate all stood back in fear. Only Ame-no-Uzume, ​goddess of dawn, mirth, and dance, stepped forward. ‌She spoke to him boldly and well, and ​the gatekeeper was won: he asked who was ‌coming and offered himself as guide. No force ​moved him and no god outranked him; what opened ‌the road was speech. The myth's meaning is ​a charter of legitimacy: heaven's claim to the ‌land passes through an earthly gatekeeper's consent — ​rule is negotiated at the threshold, not imposed ‌from the sky.[^2]

### The Marriage That Founded a ​Line (Kojiki)

After the descent was accomplished, Ame-no-Uzume ​married Sarutahiko, and the *Kojiki* draws the genealogical ‌consequence: Uzume is the ancestress of the Sarume ‌— the “monkey-women” — the order of female ‌ritual dancers of the Yamato court, whose sacred ​performances are the root from which *kagura*, and ​in part the comic spirit of Noh, descend. ‌The marriage folds the unruly leader of the earthly ​kami into the celestial order without domesticating him: ​he remains the red-faced giant, she remains the ‌dancer who out-talked him, and together they become ​the founding couple of Japanese sacred performance. Structurally ​the pairing is exact — the goddess who ‌moves between worlds weds the god who guards ​the crossing — and politically it is shrewd: ‌the oldest indigenous power of the archipelago is ​not defeated by Ninigi's line but married into ​it. The myth remembers that Japan's ritual arts ​were born at a boundary, from a negotiation.

### ​The Drowning at Azaka (Kojiki)

Even gatekeepers die. The ‌*Kojiki* records that Sarutahiko went to Ise, to ‌the Isuzu River at Azaka, where a giant ​clam closed upon his hand while he fished; ‌he fell into the water and drowned. The ​tradition speaks the event in three divine names ​given to his spirit as he sank: *Sokodokumitama*, ‌“Bottom-Reach-Spirit,” as he went to the riverbed; *Tsubutatsumitama*, ‌“Rising-Bubble Spirit,” as his breath broke the surface; ‌and *Awasakumitama*, “Bubble-Bursting Spirit,” as the bubbles burst ‌and were gone. Anthropologist Emiko Ohnuki-Tierney reads the ​episode through the monkey symbolism latent in his ‌name — the macaque with one hand trapped ​in a shell is a stock figure of Japanese ​folktale. The undertone of the myth is initiatory: ​the god of boundaries meets his own limit ‌at the water's edge, and in the telling ​of his death the river at Ise gains ​a guardian presence that outlasts the god's body.

### ​The Great Kami of the Crossroads (Folk religion)

‌Only seven kami bear the title Ōkami, “Great ​Kami,” and Sarutahiko is almost alone among them ​in being an earthly (kunitsukami) rather than a ​heavenly deity — Inari is the other. Medieval ‌Shugendō adopted him as a protector of mountain ​ascetics; later folk religion made him patron of roads, ‌travelers, comedians, and performers — his grotesque mask ​leads the *Menkake Gyōretsu*, the masked procession still ‌held at Kamakura's Tsurugaoka Hachimangū, and Ueshiba Morihei, ​founder of Aikido, made Sarutahiko's stance between heaven ‌and earth the model of aiki, standing “one ‌with the universe.” His cult geography is anchored ​by Tsubaki Grand Shrine in Mie — first ​among some two thousand branch shrines — and ​Sarutahiko Jinja beside the Isuzu River at Ise, ​near the place of his drowning. The pattern ‌across the centuries is consistent: whoever stands at ‌a threshold — pilgrim, dancer, martial artist — ​stands where Sarutahiko stood first.

sections.body: Sarutahiko's ​cult geography ‌is ‌unusually ​legible. Tsubaki ​Grand ​Shrine at ​Suzuka ​in ‌Mie Prefecture, ​set ​at the ‌foot ​of ‌Mount Nyūdō, ​is ‌the head ​shrine ​of ​his cult, ​first ​among some ‌two ​thousand ‌branch shrines; ​Sarutahiko ‌Jinja stands ​by ‌the ​Isuzu River ‌at ​Ise, beside ​the ‌river ‌of his ‌drowning, ​and Ōasahiko ​Shrine ‌in ​Tokushima is ​another ‌ancient seat. ​Images ​of ‌the god ​— ‌the ​red shining ​face, ​hanging beard, ​long ‌nose ‌— survive ​in ‌shrine statuary, ​festival ​regalia, ‌and the ‌masks ‌of the ‌Menkake ​Gyōretsu ‌procession still ​performed ​at Kamakura's ​Tsurugaoka ‌Hachimangū, ​a medieval ​rite ​whose masks ‌are ​preserved ​as temple ​treasures. ‌No inscription ​from ‌the ​archaic period ‌names ​him; his ‌earliest ‌witnesses ​are the ​Kojiki ​(712) and ​Nihon ‌Shoki ‌(720) manuscripts ​themselves.[^1]
